docs.title: Constructing and simulating molecular systems
docs.text:
Here is a brief overview of the main documentation sections:

  • Introduction – Provides a description of EasyShapes, including its purpose, licensing, latest release details, and contact information.
  • Installation & Setup – Guides users through system requirements, environment configuration, and the installation process.
  • User Guide – Covers core concepts, key terminology, workflow steps, and essential parameters for effective use of EasyShapes.
  • Tutorials – Offers practical, step-by-step examples demonstrating common workflows and data analysis tasks.

docs.title: Installation & Setup
docs.text:
EasyShapes is a cross-platform desktop application for Windows, macOS, and Linux, compatible with Python 3.11 through 3.13.

To install and set up EasyShapes, we recommend using Pixi, a modern package manager for Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Main benefits of using Pixi
  • Ease of use: Pixi simplifies the installation process, making it accessible even for users with limited experience in package management.
  • Python version control: Pixi allows specifying and managing different Python versions for each project, ensuring compatibility.
  • Isolated environments: Pixi creates isolated environments for each project, preventing conflicts between different package versions.
  • PyPI and Conda support: Pixi can install packages from both PyPI and Conda repositories, providing access to a wide range of libraries.

A packaged application, which needs no Pixi, will be available on the GitHub Releases page later.

docs.title: Installing with Pixi recommended
docs.text: This section describes the simplest way to set up EasyShapes using Pixi.

docs.title: Installing Pixi
docs.text: • Install Pixi by following the instructions on the official Pixi Installation Guide.

docs.title: Setting up EasyShapes with Pixi
docs.text:
• Check that your system is supported: Windows (64-bit), Linux (x86-64, glibc 2.35 or newer, e.g. Ubuntu 22.04+), or macOS 14 or newer on Apple Silicon.
  • Make sure Git is installed.

  • Choose a project location (local drive recommended).

    Windows + OneDrive

    We do not recommend creating a Pixi project inside OneDrive or other synced folders.

    By default, Pixi creates the virtual environment inside the project directory (in .pixi/). On Windows, synced folders such as OneDrive may cause file‑system issues (e.g., path-length limitations or restricted link operations), which can lead to unexpected install errors or environments being recreated.

    Instead, create your project in a local directory on your drive where you have full write permissions.

  • Download EasyShapes and navigate into it. Until the first release, the application is on the develop branch: 
    git clone --branch develop https://github.com/easyscience/shapes-app.git
cd shapes-app
  • Install EasyShapes and everything it needs: 
    pixi install
    This sets up the full development environment, including the tools for tests and documentation. The packaged application will be lighter.

docs.title: Running EasyShapes
docs.text:
• Start the application inside the shapes-app directory: 
    pixi run easyshapes-py

docs.title: Updating EasyShapes
docs.text:
• Get the latest version and install what it needs: 
    git pull
pixi install
    Use pixi install, not pixi update: pixi update moves to newer package versions than EasyShapes was tested with.
  • To update Pixi itself to the latest version: 
    pixi self-update

docs.title: Uninstalling EasyShapes and Pixi
docs.text:
• To remove EasyShapes, delete the shapes-app directory. Its environment is inside it, in .pixi/.
  • By default, your projects and the Shapespyer settings are saved outside that directory: in %APPDATA%\SimNavi\Shapespyer\ on Windows, in ~/Library/Application Support/Shapespyer/ on macOS, and in ~/.local/share/Shapespyer/ (projects) and ~/.config/Shapespyer/ (settings) on Linux. Delete them only if you no longer need your projects.
  • To uninstall Pixi, follow the official Pixi Guide.

docs.title: GROMACS optional
docs.text:
EasyShapes builds structures on its own. To equilibrate them (Analysis › Equilibration), it runs GROMACS, which you install yourself.

  • Install GROMACS by following the GROMACS installation guide. On Linux and macOS, package managers offer it (for example apt, Homebrew or conda-forge). On Windows, GROMACS has to be built from source; running EasyShapes inside WSL (Linux on Windows) is simpler.
  • EasyShapes runs gmx from your PATH. The Engine item in the status bar shows the GROMACS version it found, or why it can't run it.
  • If your GROMACS program has another name or is not on PATH (for example gmx_mpi), set it in the Shapespyer config.yaml, in the settings folder listed under Uninstalling: 
    gmx_executable: /path/to/gmx

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text: To work on the EasyShapes code itself (tests, formatting, documentation), see the Contributing Guidelines.

docs.title: Description
docs.text:
EasyShapes is a scientific software for generation of ordered molecular aggregates and pre-assembled composite structures to seed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations aimed at studying equilibration (relaxation) processes in soft matter and biomolecular systems.

EasyShapes is developed as a cross-platform desktop application based on Qt and QML.

docs.title: License
docs.text: EasyShapes application is released under the BSD 3-Clause License.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text:
The latest version of the EasyShapes application is maintenance.

For a complete list of new features, bug fixes, and improvements, see the GitHub Releases page.

docs.title: Citation
docs.text:
If you use EasyShapes application in your work, please cite Shapespyer, which builds its structures. Its Digital Object Identifier (DOI), for all versions, is 10.5281/zenodo.19074587.

Citation details in various styles (e.g., APA, MLA) and formats (e.g., BibTeX, JSON) are available on that Zenodo page.

The EasyShapes application will get its own DOI on Zenodo with its first release.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text:
We welcome contributions of any kind!

EasyShapes is intended to be a community-driven, open-source project supported by a diverse group of contributors.

The project is maintained by the European Spallation Source (ESS).

If you would like to report a bug or request a new feature, please use the GitHub Issue Tracker (A free GitHub account is required.)

To contribute code, documentation, or tests, please see our Contributing Guidelines for detailed development instructions.

docs.title: Questions and Feedback
docs.text: Ask questions or share feedback in GitHub Discussions, the discussion forum for the whole EasyShapes project. To report a bug, use the GitHub Issue Tracker.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial starts from a goal: the system to build and the result to aim for. Then it goes through only the controls needed to get there.

  • Multilamellar vesicle – build a dry vesicle of POPC and cholesterol with two lamellae, and prepare it for equilibration. No GROMACS needed.
  • SDS ball (micelle) – build a ball of SDS molecules with their sodium ions in water, equilibrate it briefly with GROMACS, and calculate its scattering curves.

docs.title: The goal
docs.text:
Build a dry multilamellar vesicle of POPC and cholesterol, 70 : 30, with two lamellae. Then prepare it for equilibration: restrain the lipids and set the temperature.

The spacing comes from neutron scattering on POPC vesicles. The lamellae repeat every 6.4 nm in pure POPC (Holme et al., ACS Cent. Sci. 2018, 10.1021/acscentsci.8b00286), and 30 mol% cholesterol adds 0.23 nm (Utterström et al., Bioconjugate Chem. 2022, 10.1021/acs.bioconjchem.2c00115). So the lamellae here repeat every 6.6 nm: a bilayer of about 4 nm and 2.6 nm of space for water.

Setting Lamella 1 Lamella 2 Rmin, nm 3.0 9.6 Inner dmin, nm 0.65 0.65 Outer dmin, nm 0.85 0.85 Shell thickness, nm 4.0 4.0 POPC : CHL 70 : 30 70 : 30

The dmins give the two-tail lipids more room than the default 0.5 nm. The result holds 3,600 POPC and 1,543 cholesterol molecules in a 28.5 nm box.

The vesicle stays dry, so this tutorial needs no GROMACS. Running the equilibration needs water and GROMACS; Tutorial 2 shows a run.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Install EasyShapes, see Installation & Setup.
  • GROMACS is not needed. The status bar may show "gmx not found".
  • A laptop is enough. The assembly takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Create the project
docs.text:
1. On the Home page, click Start. The Project page opens.
  2. Click Create a new project.
  3. In the Create project dialog, set Name to MLV and click OK. An empty Location saves the project in the default projects folder.
  4. Click Continue. The Sample Model page opens.

docs.title: Choose the shape
docs.text:
On the Sample Model page, in Basic controls › Model Definition:

  1. Set Shape to Vesicle.
  2. Keep Type at Discrete.

The Vesicle Structure Definition and Lamellae groups appear.

docs.title: Add the components
docs.text:
In Basic controls › Components:

  1. Click Load component(s).
  2. In the list, click POPC, then Ctrl+click CHL. Click OK.

The table shows POPC and CHL.

docs.title: Set the lamellae
docs.text:
In Basic controls › Lamellae:

  1. Click Add lamella. The table now has two rows.
  2. In row 1, set Rmin, nm to 3, Inner dmin, nm to 0.65, Outer dmin, nm to 0.85 and Shell thickness, nm to 4.
  3. In row 2, set the same values, but Rmin, nm to 9.6.
  4. Select row 1. In the Fractions table below, set the Mole ratio of POPC to 70 and of CHL to 30.
  5. Select row 2 and set the same ratios.

The main area's Shape tab shows both lamellae, each with "shell 4.00 nm".

docs.title: Assemble
docs.text:
Click Assemble, below the groups. The main area switches to the Structure tab and shows the progress. It takes a few minutes.

While it assembles

Shapespyer places the molecules ring by ring on each leaflet's sphere, at least dmin apart, and then writes the structure file.

The library's POPC is straight and about 2.95 nm long. Two of them don't fit in a 4 nm shell, so the leaflets start overlapping. During equilibration the tails bend and get shorter, and the bilayer settles near the measured thickness.

The 2.6 nm between the lamellae is where water goes when the vesicle is solvated.

docs.title: Save the project
docs.text: Press Ctrl+S, or click at the top left. The first save creates the project folder and copies the files of the components and of the configuration into it. Save before you edit any file: until then, opens the asset library's own file, and a change there reaches every new project.

docs.title: Restrain heads and tail ends
docs.text:
During equilibration, position restraints hold chosen atoms near reference positions while everything else relaxes. Here each lipid's head and one tail end are restrained. That keeps the molecules pointing outward and the leaflets in place. Restrain only one tail: two restrained tails can cause more clashes in a packed lamella.

The library's POPC and cholesterol have no restraints. You add them to each component's topology file (.itp).

docs.title: Find the atoms
docs.text:
On the Sample Model page, open the main area's Components tab and pick POPC in Component. Hover over an atom to see its number and element, for example 19 (P). Click an atom to keep its label.

The viewer counts atoms from 0, and the .itp file counts from 1, so add 1 to the viewer's number. The viewer shows the element, not the atom's name.

  • POPC: the phosphorus shows 19 (P), so it is atom 20. The last carbon of the longer tail shows 87 (C), so it is atom 88.
  • Cholesterol: the only oxygen shows 2 (O), so it is atom 3. The tail ends in two carbons, C26 and C27. This tutorial uses C27, which shows 70 (C), so it is atom 71.

docs.title: Check them in the topology file
docs.text:
In Advanced controls › Components Files, set Select component to POPC. Click next to POPC_DLF.itp. It opens in your system's default app for .itp files. If the system asks which app to use, pick a text editor such as Notepad.

You saved the project, so this is its own copy of the file.

Near the top of the file, the [ atoms ] list has one line per atom of the molecule. It came with the component from the asset library: DL_FIELD made it for the CHARMM36 force field. The first column, nr, is the atom's number, and the fifth, atom, is its name:

[ atoms ]
; nr   type   resnr   residu    atom    cgnr    charge    mass
    1      NTL    1 POPC    N     1  -0.6000000   14.0067
...
   20       PL    1 POPC    P    20   1.5000000   30.9740
...
   88     CTL3    1 POPC C218    88  -0.2700000   12.0110

So atom 20 is P, the head, and atom 88 is C218, the end of the oleoyl tail.

A ; starts a comment: GROMACS ignores the rest of the line. The second line is a comment that names the columns, as a reminder for you.

docs.title: Add the restraints
docs.text:
At the end of POPC_DLF.itp, add these lines and save the file:

#ifdef POSRES
[ position_restraints ]
;  ai  funct  fcx            fcy            fcz
   20      1  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; P, head
   88      1  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C218, tail end
#endif

Then set Select component to CHL, open CHL.itp the same way, and add at its end:

#ifdef POSRES
[ position_restraints ]
;  ai  funct  fcx            fcy            fcz
    3      1  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; O3, head
   71      1  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C27, tail end
#endif

What the lines mean:

  • #ifdef POSRES … #endif – GROMACS reads the block only in the stages whose .mdp file defines POSRES: equil1 to equil4. The energy minimisation, equil0, and the last stages, equil5 and equil6, run without restraints.
  • ai – the atom's number from [ atoms ].
  • funct – 1 is a harmonic spring that pulls the atom back to its reference position.
  • fcx, fcy, fcz – the spring's force constant along x, y and z. POSRES_FC_LIP is a name; each stage's .mdp file gives its value: 200, 100, 50 and 20 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻². The springs get weaker stage by stage.
  • ; P, head – a comment that says which atom the line holds.

docs.title: Two ways to restrain
docs.text:
The reference position, where a spring pulls to, depends on Restrain to box centre on the Analysis page, in Basic controls › Equilibration:

  • Unticked – each atom is held where it is when the stage starts. This tutorial uses this way.
  • Ticked – the reference of every restrained atom is the centre of the box.

Each way goes with its own funct:

Restrain to box centre funct What it does Use it for Unticked 1, harmonic Pulls each atom back to its position at the start of the stage Any shape, any number of lamellae Unticked 2, flat-bottom, small radius Lets each atom move freely up to the radius from its start; pulls it back beyond A start that is nearly right but needs room Ticked 2, flat-bottom, sphere radius Lets each atom move freely within the radius of the box centre; pulls it back beyond. A negative radius keeps the atom outside instead A vesicle with one lamella, or a ball Ticked 1, harmonic Pulls every restrained atom to the centre of the box Nothing: don't combine these

A flat-bottom line has the columns ai, funct (2), g (1 for a sphere), r (the radius, nm) and k (the force constant). Two lines for one atom, one with a positive and one with a negative radius, keep it in a spherical shell. For example, for a cholesterol head between 4.5 and 8.5 nm from the centre of a vesicle with one lamella:

;  ai  funct  g     r   k
    1      2  1   8.5   POSRES_FC_LIP   ; within 8.5 nm of the centre
    1      2  1  -4.5   POSRES_FC_LIP   ; at least 4.5 nm from it

This tutorial can't use the shell way. One .itp file holds the restraints for every POPC, in both lamellae, so one set of radii can't fit two lamellae at different distances from the centre.

docs.title: Set the temperature
docs.text:
1. On the Sample Model page, click Continue. The Analysis page opens.
  2. In Advanced controls › Configuration Files, click next to equil1.mdp.
  3. Change ref_t from 310 to 298.15 (25 °C, the temperature of the measurements) and save the file.
  4. Do the same in equil2.mdp to equil6.mdp.

equil0.mdp is the energy minimisation: it has no temperature.

In equil1.mdp to equil5.mdp, the lines look like this:

tcoupl                  = berendsen
tc_grps                 = SYSTEM
tau_t                   = 1.0
ref_t                   = 310

After the change:

tcoupl                  = berendsen
tc_grps                 = SYSTEM
tau_t                   = 1.0
ref_t                   = 298.15

equil6.mdp has two ref_t lines. Change only the one without ; at the start. The other one is a comment:

;tcoupl                  = berendsen
;tc_grps                 = SYSTEM
;tau_t                   = 1.0
;ref_t                   = 310
;
tcoupl                  = nose-hoover ;berendsen
tc_grps                 = SYSTEM
tau_t                   = 1.0
ref_t                   = 298.15

The ;berendsen after nose-hoover is also a comment: an older choice, kept as a note.

The other settings in these files, such as the pressure coupling, are already right.

docs.title: Choose per-atom restraints
docs.text:
On the Analysis page, in Basic controls › Equilibration, leave Restrain to box centre unticked.

Don't click Equilibrate: the vesicle has no water, and the run needs GROMACS.

docs.title: Save again
docs.text: Press Ctrl+S again. The project folder now holds the vesicle, the restraints and the temperatures.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The vesicle needs water before it can be equilibrated. Tutorial 2 shows how to add a buffer, run the equilibration and calculate a scattering curve, with a ball of SDS.

docs.title: The goal
docs.text:
Build a ball of SDS (sodium dodecyl sulfate) molecules with their sodium counter-ions in water: a model of an SDS micelle. Equilibrate it briefly with GROMACS, then calculate two small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) curves: one in heavy water (D₂O), and one in light water (H₂O) with deuterated SDS.

The ball follows Shapespyer's SDS ball tutorial: one layer with 16 molecules on its equator, 0.4 nm apart. So Rmin is 16 × 0.4 / 2π, about 1.02 nm.

The assembled ball holds 80 SDS molecules, 80 sodium ions and about 4,900 water molecules: 18,212 atoms.

The equilibration runs two stages: an energy minimisation (eq0) and 25 ps of molecular dynamics with restraints (eq1). That takes minutes.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
• Install EasyShapes and GROMACS (Linux, macOS, or WSL on Windows), see Installation & Setup. The status bar shows whether the app found GROMACS.
  • This tutorial edits a topology file the way the vesicle tutorial explains. Read that one first.

docs.title: Create the project
docs.text:
1. On the Home page, click Start.
  2. Click Create a new project, set Name to SDSBall and click OK.
  3. Click Continue. The Sample Model page opens.

docs.title: Build the ball
docs.text:
In Basic controls › Model Definition, set Shape to Ball. Keep Type at Discrete.

In Basic controls › Components:

  1. Click Load component(s), click SDS in the list and click OK.
  2. In the SDS row, set C-ion to NAT. Each SDS gets one sodium ion.

In Basic controls › Layers, set Dmin, nm to 0.4 and Rmin, nm to 1.02 in row 1.

In Basic controls › Buffer, set Solvent to TIP3.

docs.title: Save and assemble
docs.text:
Press Ctrl+S to save the project. As in the vesicle tutorial, save before you edit any file.

Click Assemble. Shapespyer places the molecules, and GROMACS adds the sodium ions and the water. The main area shows the Structure tab.

docs.title: Restrain the tails
docs.text:
In eq1, restraints keep the micelle's core together while the water settles. Here they act on the tail carbons and are anchored at the centre of the box: the second way in the vesicle tutorial's table.

In Advanced controls › Components Files, set Select component to SDS and click next to SDS.itp. At its end, the library's file restrains only the sulfur atom:

#ifdef POSRES
[ position_restraints ]
    1     1    POSRES_FC_LIP    POSRES_FC_LIP    POSRES_FC_LIP
#endif

Replace these lines with the restraints of Shapespyer's SDS ball example, and save the file:

#ifdef POSRES
[ position_restraints ]
;  ai  funct  g    r  k
    9      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C2
   15      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C4
   21      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C6
   27      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C8
   33      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C10
   39      2  1  2.0  POSRES_FC_LIP   ; C12, the tail end
#endif

What the new lines mean:

  • ai – every second carbon of the tail, C2 to C12, by its number in the file's [ atoms ] list.
  • funct 2 – a flat-bottom restraint.
  • g 1 – its shape: a sphere.
  • r 2.0 – the sphere's radius, in nm. Inside it the atom moves freely. Outside it, a spring pulls the atom back.
  • k – the spring's force constant. Each stage's .mdp file sets it: 200 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻² in eq1.

With Restrain to box centre ticked (next section), the spheres sit at the centre of the box. So every restrained carbon stays within 2 nm of the centre, and the core holds together.

docs.title: Equilibrate
docs.text:
1. Click Continue. The Analysis page opens.
  2. In Basic controls › Equilibration, keep Configuration and Force field at CHARMM36.
  3. Keep First stage at eq0, and set Last stage to eq1.
  4. Tick Restrain to box centre.
  5. Click Equilibrate. The Engine output tab shows the GROMACS commands and their output while the run goes on.

While it runs

eq0 minimises the energy: it moves the atoms out of each other's way, without restraints.

eq1 runs 25 ps of molecular dynamics at 310 K, with the tail restraints at 200 kJ mol⁻¹ nm⁻².

The configuration's later stages lower the restraints step by step and then run without them, for a better relaxed micelle. They take much longer.

docs.title: Look at the result
docs.text: Open the main area's Structure tab and set Stage to eq1.

docs.title: Calculate the curves
docs.text:
In Basic controls › Scattering:

  1. Set Structure to eq1.
  2. Set Solvent SLD, 10⁻⁶ Å⁻² to 6.36, for D₂O, and click Calculate.
  3. Set Solvent SLD, 10⁻⁶ Å⁻² to −0.56, for H₂O, tick SDS under Deuterate, and click Calculate.

Keep the other fields at their defaults.

Why these two curves

The calculation scatters from the SDS atoms only. The water and the ions count as a uniform solvent, without a hydration shell.

In D₂O, the hydrogen-rich tails stand out strongly against the heavy water: a common SANS measurement of SDS micelles. In H₂O, deuterated tails stand out just as strongly against the light water. The tails dominate both curves. The head groups have a different contrast in each, so the curves differ where the head-group shell matters.

docs.title: Read the curves
docs.text: The Scattering tab draws both curves. In Advanced controls › Scattering view, the Rg, Å column gives each curve's radius of gyration. Tick Staggered view to draw the second curve lower, so the two don't overlap.

docs.title: Save
docs.text: Press Ctrl+S.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: The User Guide's Analysis page describes every control used here.

docs.title: User Guide
docs.text: EasyShapes builds ordered molecular aggregates, such as vesicles, bilayers and micelles, as starting structures for molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. It can then equilibrate them with GROMACS and calculate their small-angle neutron scattering (SANS).

docs.title: Workflow
docs.text:
The tabs at the top of the window lead through the work, from left to right. Each tab after Home has its own page, which describes every group and control on it:

  1. Home – click Start to open the Project page.
  2. Project – create a new project, open an existing one, or start from an example or a recent project.
  3. Sample Model – choose the structure type, add the components (molecules) and their fractions, set the structure's layers or lamellae and the buffer, then click Assemble. Continue opens the Analysis page.
  4. Analysis – equilibrate the structure with GROMACS (Equilibrate) and calculate its scattering curves (Calculate). Continue opens the Summary page.
  5. Summary – read an outline of the project and its results.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Each tutorial starts from a goal: the system to build and the result to aim for. Then it goes through only the controls needed to get there.

  • Multilamellar vesicle – build a dry vesicle of POPC and cholesterol with two lamellae, and prepare it for equilibration. No GROMACS needed.
  • SDS ball (micelle) – build a ball of SDS molecules with their sodium ions in water, equilibrate it briefly with GROMACS, and calculate its scattering curves.

docs.title: Analysis
docs.text:
The Analysis page equilibrates the assembled structure with GROMACS and calculates its small-angle neutron scattering (SANS) curves.

The sidebar on the right has two tabs:

  • Basic controls – the equilibration and the scattering calculation.
  • Advanced controls – their files, the structure viewer's settings and the list of curves.

The main area on the left shows Engine output (the GROMACS log), Structure (a stage's atoms) and Scattering (the curves).

Continue, at the bottom of the sidebar, opens the Summary page.

docs.title: Equilibration
docs.text:
The equilibration runs the stages of a configuration one after another. Stage k runs the configuration's equil<k>.mdp, starting where the stage before ended. Stage eq0 starts from the assembled structure.

  • Configuration – the .mdp files from the asset library, such as CHARMM36.
  • Force field – the force field from the asset library.
  • First stage – eq0, or a stage after one that has finished.
  • Last stage – the stage to stop after.
  • Threads – how many threads mdrun runs on. Empty lets mdrun choose.
  • Restrain to box centre – anchors the position restraints of the structure's components at the centre of the box. Unticked, each restrained atom is held where it is when the stage starts. The vesicle tutorial explains both ways.

Equilibrate starts the run. It needs GROMACS (see Installation & Setup). Cancel equilibration stops it. The Engine output tab shows the progress.

docs.title: Scattering
docs.text:
Calculates the SANS curve of a structure. It needs no GROMACS.

  • Structure – the assembled sample model, or a finished stage of the equilibration.
  • Kernel – Exact works for any shape, but can be slow. Fast can take seconds even for a million atoms, but use it only for round aggregates.
  • Solvent SLD, 10⁻⁶ Å⁻² – the scattering length density of the solvent around the aggregate, buffer salts included. H₂O is −0.56, D₂O 6.36.
  • q min, Å⁻¹ and q max, Å⁻¹ – the q range of the curve. Both above 0, and q min below q max.
  • q points – how many q values, evenly spaced on a log scale. At least 5.
  • Polydispersity – the spread of aggregate sizes, σ/R. 0 is one size. 0.25 puts about 2 in 3 aggregates within ±25 % of the simulated size.
  • Deuterate – tick the components that are deuterated.

Calculate starts the calculation, and Cancel calculation stops it. The new curve is added to Scattering view.

docs.title: Configuration Files
docs.text:
The configuration's .mdp files, with their sizes. opens a file in your system's default app. removes it. Add new file(s), Save to lib and Export work as in the Sample Model page's Library assets. Only files named equil<k>.mdp run, each as stage k.

Until the project's first save, the configuration is the asset library's own copy. Save the project before you edit a file.

docs.title: Force Field Files
docs.text: The same, for the force field's files. Each run uses the force field's first .itp file.

docs.title: Equilibration Files
docs.text:
The files of the equilibration and of each finished stage, picked in Files of. The equilibration holds its copies of the model and the topologies (toppar/), and its log. A stage holds the files GROMACS wrote for it.

  • opens a file in your system's default app.
  • Export – copies the selected file to a folder, or all the files shown when none is selected.
  • Open folder – opens the folder of the files in your system's file browser.

Each Equilibrate copies toppar/ and the model's .gro and .top again, so changes to these copies are lost. Edit the components on the Sample Model page, or the force field, instead.

docs.title: Structure viewer
docs.text: The settings of the Sample Model page's Structure viewer, for this page's Structure tab.

docs.title: Scattering view
docs.text:
The curves calculated so far, one row each:

  • Curve – the curve's name, with its colour. Hover over the name to see how it was calculated.
  • Status – done, or outdated once its structure has changed.
  • Rg, Å – the radius of gyration.
  • Show – draws the curve in the Scattering tab.
  • – removes the curve and its files.

Below the list:

  • Staggered view – draws each further curve lower, by the decades set on the slider, so overlapping curves come apart. Only the chart changes.
  • Export data – writes one .dat file per shown curve to a folder.
  • Export as PNG – saves the Scattering tab's chart and legend as a PNG image.

docs.title: Engine output
docs.text: A log, picked in Log at the top right. Equilibration shows each GROMACS command of the latest run and its output, while it grows. Each run starts it anew. A finished stage shows its mdrun log.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: A structure, picked in Stage at the top right: the equilibration's copy of the assembled model, or the final structure of a finished stage. The Structure viewer group sets the slab and the look. The mouse controls are those of the Sample Model page.

docs.title: Scattering
docs.text: The curves ticked Show in Scattering view: I(q) in cm⁻¹ against q in Å⁻¹, both on log scales. The buttons at the top right show or hide the legend, show the values under the cursor, switch on pan or box zoom, and reset the axes. A right-click on the chart also resets them.

docs.title: Project
docs.text:
A project holds everything you make in EasyShapes: the sample model, its assembled structure, and the analysis with its equilibration and scattering results. Each project is a folder on disk.

Start on the Home page opens this page.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
• Create a new project – opens the Create project dialog (below).
  • Open an existing project – opens a project folder.

Creating or opening a project replaces the open one without asking, so save your work first.

The Create project dialog has three fields. All are optional:

  • Name – starts with a letter, then 1–30 letters, digits, _, - or .. Empty gives a random name.
  • Description – a short note about the project.
  • Location – the folder to save the project in. picks one. It must be new or empty. Empty saves to Projects/<name>-<ID> in Shapespyer's data folder (see Installation & Setup for where it is).

The new project is written to disk at its first save.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Ready-made projects to start from. Click one to open it. Saving it saves a copy in the default projects folder, and the example stays as it is.

docs.title: Recent projects
docs.text: The projects you have saved, newest first. Click one to open it.

docs.title: Description tab
docs.text:
The open project:

  • Name – the large title. Click it to change it, with the same rule as in the Create project dialog.
  • Description – click it to change it.
  • Location – the project's folder.

docs.title: Saving
docs.text: at the top left of the window, or Ctrl+S, saves the project into its folder. The first save creates the folder, copies the files of the sample model and the analysis into it, and adds the project to Recent projects.

docs.title: Continue
docs.text:
Continue opens the Sample Model page.

Without a project, the button reads Continue without project. You can build a sample model then, but not save it. A project you create afterwards keeps that sample model.

docs.title: Sample Model
docs.text:
The Sample Model page defines what to build: the structure's shape, its components (molecules), how they are arranged, and the buffer around them. Assemble then builds the structure's coordinates with Shapespyer.

The sidebar on the right has two tabs:

  • Basic controls – what to build.
  • Advanced controls – the files behind it: the asset library, the components' files, the assembled model's files, the SMILES generator and the structure viewer's settings.

The main area on the left shows the model: Shape (a sketch of the structure), Components (each molecule in 3D) and Structure (the assembled atoms). A lattice model adds a Lattice tab.

Continue, at the bottom of the sidebar, opens the Analysis page.

docs.title: Model Definition
docs.text:
One row for the project's sample model:

  • Name – the model's name. The name matters when you save the model to the asset library or load it from there.
  • Type – Discrete builds one structure. Lattice repeats it on a lattice and shows the Lattice Parameters group. Switching back to Discrete drops the lattice settings.
  • Shape – Ring, Ball, Vesicle, Rod, Bilayer or Monolayer. A new shape keeps the components, but its structure settings start from the defaults.

Below the row:

  • Load model – replaces the model with one saved in the asset library.
  • Import model – replaces the model with one from a folder, for example one a colleague exported with Sample Model Files › Export.

docs.title: Components
docs.text:
The molecules the structure is made of. One row per component:

  • Name – a unique name, the residue name in the component's structure file.
  • Type – Lipid, Surfactant or Component. Set in the asset library.
  • C-ion – the counter-ion that goes with each molecule, from the ions in the asset library. Empty for none.
  • Mint and Mext – the indices of two atoms of the molecule, counted from 0. The line from Mint to Mext, its "bone", sets how the molecule is placed: Mint points into the structure, Mext out of it. Hover over an atom in the main area's Components tab to see its index.
  • – removes the component from the project. The asset library and the files on disk keep it.

Below the table:

  • Load component(s) – adds one or more components from the asset library.
  • Import component – adds a component from a folder, for example one exported with Components Files › Export.

docs.title: Fractions
docs.text:
A Fractions table says how much of each component goes into a part of the structure. Ring, Rod, Bilayer and Monolayer have one, in their structure group. A ball has one per layer, and a vesicle one per lamella or leaflet. One row per component:

  • Present – tick to place the component here.
  • Component name – the name from the Components group.
  • Mole ratio – 0 or more. Ratios are relative: 70 and 30 give the same mix as 7 and 3.

docs.title: Structure definition
docs.text:
Each shape has its own … Structure Definition group. Distances are in nm, angles in degrees. A value that can't be built turns red.

Several shapes share these controls:

  • Dmin – the smallest distance between the bones of neighbouring molecules.
  • Rmin – the radius of the empty space in the middle.
  • Fxz – first flattens each molecule into the XZ plane, so it spreads less along Y.
  • Rev – swaps Mint and Mext, so the molecules point the other way.
  • Fill (Ball and Vesicle) – how the molecules cover the sphere. FIBO spreads them evenly along a Fibonacci spiral. RINGS0 places them on rings of latitude, the same above and below the equator. RINGS also uses rings of latitude, often denser, but not always the same above and below.

docs.title: Ring
docs.text:
One ring of molecules. Dmin, Rmin, Fxz and Rev, plus:

  • Alpha – the starting angle of the molecules in the XY plane, 0–360°.
  • Theta – their tilt from the Z axis, 0–180°.
  • Ring Fractions.

Rmin must be at least half of Dmin, or it turns red.

docs.title: Ball
docs.text: A sphere of one or more layers. Fill, Fxz and Rev, plus Full radius, the radius of the whole ball.

docs.title: Vesicle
docs.text: A sphere of one or more lamellae, each a bilayer. Fill, Fxz and Rev, plus Full radius, the radius of the whole vesicle.

docs.title: Rod
docs.text:
A stack of rings with a half-sphere cap at each end. Dmin, Rmin, Fxz and Rev, plus:

  • Turns – how many rings are stacked, Dmin apart.
  • Rod Fractions.

Rmin must be at least 1.6 times Dmin, or it turns red.

docs.title: Bilayer
docs.text:
A flat, square patch of two leaflets:

  • Zsep – the distance between the two leaflets' Mext atoms. At 0, their Mint atoms are placed Dmin apart instead.
  • Nside – how many molecules along each side of the square. The patch is Nside × Dmin wide.
  • Dmin.
  • Bilayer Fractions.

docs.title: Monolayer
docs.text: The same controls as Bilayer, but the molecules point the other way: the two sheets face each other with their Mext atoms, Zsep apart (Dmin apart at 0).

docs.title: Layers
docs.text:
Shown for a ball. One row per layer, from the inside out:

  • Dmin, nm – the smallest distance between molecules in the layer.
  • Rmin, nm – the layer's inner radius.
  • Thickness, nm – the length of the longest molecule in the layer.
  • – removes the layer.

Rmin must be at least 1.6 times Dmin, or both turn red: Shapespyer can't build that. Add layer adds one. Select a row to set its fractions below the table.

docs.title: Lamellae
docs.text:
Shown for a vesicle. One row per lamella, from the inside out:

  • Rmin, nm – the lamella's inner radius.
  • Inner dmin, nm and Outer dmin, nm – the smallest distance between molecules in the inner and in the outer leaflet.
  • Shell thickness, nm – from Rmin to the end of the outer leaflet. It is set from the molecules when you add the lamella, and you can change it. A thin shell crowds the leaflets.
  • Symmetric – both leaflets have the same fractions. Untick it to set the outer leaflet's fractions on their own.
  • – removes the lamella.

Each leaflet's radius must be at least 1.6 times its dmin, or its cells turn red. Add lamella adds one. Select a row to set its fractions below the table.

docs.title: Lattice Parameters
docs.text:
Shown when the model's Type is Lattice. The structure is one unit, and the lattice repeats it:

  • Alpha and Theta – turn every unit: Alpha about the Z axis (0–360°), Theta up from the XY plane (0–180°).
  • Sbuff – the space between neighbouring units, in nm.
  • Type – LCUB simple cubic, LBCC body-centred cubic, LFCC face-centred cubic, or LHCP hexagonal close packing.
  • Nlatx, Nlaty, Nlatz – how many cells along X, Y and Z.

docs.title: Buffer
docs.text:
What surrounds the structure:

  • Solvent – a solvent from the asset library, such as TIP3 water. Empty for none.
  • Buffer Components – the salts in the solvent, with their Concentration, mM. removes one.
  • Load components – adds one or more salts from the asset library.
  • Import components – adds them from a folder.

The online asset library has no salts yet. To make one, such as NaCl from the ions NAT and CLA, use Library assets › Create new with the type Salt.

docs.title: Assemble
docs.text:
Assemble, below the groups, builds the structure with Shapespyer. It runs in the background, and the main area switches to the Structure tab. Cancel assembly stops it.

Adding a solvent, salts or counter-ions needs GROMACS. The status bar shows whether the app has found it (see Installation & Setup). A dry structure assembles without it.

Big structures take time: a vesicle of about 1.8 million atoms takes a few minutes on a laptop.

docs.title: Library assets
docs.text:
The asset library holds what the Load buttons in Basic controls offer. This group creates and changes its entries:

  • Create new – starts a new asset.
  • Load from lib – opens an asset from the library to change it.
  • Type – Lipid, Surfactant, Component, Ion, Solvent or Salt.
  • Name – the asset's name in the library.
  • C-ion, Mint, Mext – for Lipid, Surfactant and Component, as in the Components group. They are the defaults a loaded component starts with.
  • Salt composition – for a Salt, instead of files: the Cation and the Anion, from the library's ions, and how many of each (Count).
  • The files of the asset, with their Path and Size. opens a file in your system's default app for its type. removes it from the asset.
  • Add new file – adds files from disk: structure files (.gro, .pdb, .xyz), topology files (.itp, .top) or SMILES files (.sml).
  • Save to lib – saves the asset to the library. Components already in the project don't change. Load them again to use the new version.
  • Export – copies the selected file to a folder, or the whole asset when no file is selected.

docs.title: Components Files
docs.text:
The same as Library assets, but for the components in the project:

  • Select component – one of the components in Basic controls.
  • Name – renames it, with the same checks as the Components table.
  • Add new component – adds an empty component. Rename it, then add its files.
  • The component's files, with and as in Library assets.
  • Add new file(s), Save to lib and Export – as in Library assets, for the selected component.

Until the project's first save, a component loaded from the asset library still uses the library's files. would then change the library's own copy, which every new project uses. Save the project before you edit a file.

docs.title: Sample Model Files
docs.text:
The sample model's own files, such as the assembled structure, with their sizes:

  • opens a file in your system's default app. removes it from the model.
  • Add new file(s) – adds files from disk.
  • Save to lib – saves the model, with its components and buffer, to the asset library.
  • Export – copies the model, with its components and buffer, to a folder. Import model in Basic controls reads such a folder.

docs.title: SMILES generator
docs.text:
Builds a component from a SMILES string:

  • Name – the residue name, up to 5 letters or digits.
  • Formula – optional.
  • SMILES – the molecule, for example CCCCCCCCCCCCOS(=O)(=O)[O-] for the dodecyl sulfate ion of SDS.
  • Box (Lx, Ly, Lz) – the box size of the structure file, in nm.
  • Cis C=C – makes C=C double bonds cis instead of trans.
  • Align Z – turns the molecule so a bond at one of its ends lies along Z.
  • Flatten XZ – flattens the aligned molecule into the XZ plane. Only with Align Z.
  • Type – Lipid, Surfactant or Component.
  • Format – the structure file's format, .gro or .pdb.
  • Generate – builds the structure file and adds the new component to the project. Then set its Mint and Mext in the Components group. To save or share it, use Components Files.

docs.title: Structure viewer
docs.text:
Settings for the main area's Structure tab:

  • Background – Theme, Black, White or Grey 50%.
  • Slab plane – the plane the slab lies in: YZ, XZ or XY.
  • Lighting – Default, Volumetric, Vol-tint, Hygge or Outline.
  • Slab thickness – how much of the structure is shown, as a share of its size across the slab plane.
  • Continuous update – cuts the slab while the slider moves. This is slow for millions of atoms.
  • Keep structure loaded – when off, the structure is read again each time the Structure tab opens, and the slab starts at 5 %.
  • Show bonds – draws the bonds between atoms, from the components' .itp files. This takes about three times the graphics memory of the atoms alone.
  • Residue list – untick a residue to hide its atoms.

docs.title: Main area
docs.text: The 3D views (Components, Structure and Lattice) take the same mouse controls: drag with the left button to turn, drag with the right button to move, and use the wheel to zoom.

docs.title: Shape
docs.text:
A sketch of the structure from its current settings, drawn without assembling it. Each component's bone is an arrow from Mint to Mext, spaced Dmin apart along the structure:

  • Ring and Rod – one ring.
  • Ball – one ring per layer.
  • Vesicle – two leaflets per lamella, with the shell.
  • Bilayer and Monolayer – two flat leaflets.

The lower left shows the whole unit with its sizes. The tick boxes at the top add Component names, Dimensions (the distances and radii), and Molecules (each molecule drawn along its bone). The pictures in Basic controls above show this tab next to each group.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: One component in 3D, picked in the Component list at the top right. A gold arrow goes from its Mint atom to its Mext atom, both labelled. Hover over an atom to see its index and element. Click it to keep the label. The index counts from 0, as Mint and Mext do. A topology (.itp) file counts atoms from 1.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text: The assembled structure, atom by atom, cut to a slab. The Structure viewer group sets the slab and the look. While an assembly runs, this tab shows its progress.

docs.title: Lattice
docs.text: Shown when the model's Type is Lattice. Each unit of the lattice is a simple shape: a disc for a ring, a sphere for a ball or a vesicle, a pill for a rod, and a box for a bilayer or a monolayer.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
The Summary page shows the open project as an indented list: its name and description, the sample model with its structure and components, and the analysis. These are the settings a save writes to the project's record. The page reads the project again each time you open it, so it shows your latest changes.

Continue on the Analysis page opens this page.

You can select the text and copy it. If the project can't be listed, the reason shows in red instead.

The Export summary group in the sidebar is off in this version.
